categories: ["เงื่อนไขทางนรีเวช"]
synonyms: ["Uterine Tissue Growth Outside The Uterus", "Endometriosis (Cold Type)"]
conventional_description: Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, commonly on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and pelvic lining. It causes chronic pelvic pain, painful periods, pain during intercourse, and often infertility. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through laparoscopy, though symptoms and imaging may suggest it. The exact cause is unknown, but retrograde menstruation and immune factors are thought to play a role.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments include pain medications (NSAIDs), hormonal therapies (birth control pills, GnRH agonists, progestins) to suppress ovulation and reduce lesion activity, and surgical removal of endometrial implants. In severe cases, hysterectomy may be considered. These approaches aim to manage symptoms but do not cure the condition, and recurrence is common after stopping hormonal treatment or surgery.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees endometriosis primarily as a form of Blood Stasis - tissue that has left its proper place and formed painful masses in the pelvis. The uterus and its governing channels (the Directing and Penetrating Vessels) rely on the smooth flow of Qi and Blood, which is managed by the Liver, Kidneys, and Spleen. When emotional stress, overwork, or constitutional weakness disrupts this flow, Blood congeals and accumulates, creating the nodules and pain characteristic of the condition.
Different patterns explain why the stasis occurs. Liver Qi stagnation from frustration or stress is the most common driver, leading to Qi and Blood Stagnation with sharp, fixed pain and dark clots. Chronic fatigue or illness can weaken Qi so it can no longer push Blood, resulting in Qi Deficiency with Blood Stagnation - a dull, dragging ache. Inflammatory processes or latent Heat can combine with stasis, creating Heat and Blood Stagnation with burning pain and night sweats. When the Spleen is weak, Dampness and Phlegm mix with Stasis, forming larger cysts and masses.
This is why the same Western diagnosis of endometriosis can have very different TCM roots. A woman whose pain flares with stress and anger has a different pattern than one whose pain worsens when she's exhausted, or one who feels a constant burning sensation. Treatment must match the pattern to be effective.
classical_quote: 「妇人腹中诸疾痛，当归芍药散主之。」
classical_translation: "For various abdominal pains in women, Dang Gui Shao Yao San governs. This indicates that blood stasis and Dampness are common causes of pelvic pain, a principle applied to endometriosis today."
classical_source:
Jin Gui Yao Lue (Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Coffer)  ,  Chapter 22: Women's Miscellaneous Diseases Pulse, Symptom Complex and Treatment 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening to the story of a person’s pain and cycle. They will ask about the nature, location, and timing of the pelvic pain, the appearance of menstrual blood, and any emotional or lifestyle triggers. These clues help narrow down which pattern of stagnation is driving the endometriosis.
If the pain is sharp, stabbing, and fixed in one spot, and it worsens with stress or emotional upset, Qi and Blood Stagnation is likely. The tongue often looks dark purple with stasis spots, and the pulse feels wiry and choppy.
When fatigue and a dragging sensation dominate, with periods that feel heavy but the blood is dark and clotted, Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation may be the root. The tongue appears pale and puffy with stasis speckles, and the pulse is weak and thready.
If the pain is burning, the flow is heavy with dark clots, and there is a sensation of heat in the lower abdomen, Heat and Blood Stagnation in the Lower Burner is suspected. The tongue is reddish-purple with stasis spots and a dry yellow coating, and the pulse is deep, choppy, and rapid.
When larger masses or cysts are found, and the person also experiences bloating, heaviness, and a thick vaginal discharge, Blood Stagnation and Phlegm in the Uterus is considered. The tongue is swollen with a greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery or wiry.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pelvic pain", "Pain worse with pressure", "Dark, clotted menstrual blood", "Breast distension and irritability before period", "Purple tongue with stasis spots"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and anger, Sedentary lifestyle, Cold, raw foods and drinks, Alcohol, Suppressing emotions
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise or movement, Gentle warmth on abdomen, Stress management and emotional calm, Acupuncture
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When emotional stress, frustration, or constitutional tendencies cause the Liver Qi to stagnate, it can no longer properly move Blood. Over time, the stuck Qi leads to Blood stasis in the pelvis, forming the painful nodules, cysts, and adhesions characteristic of endometriosis. This is why the pain is often sharp and fixed.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger cause Liver Qi to stagnate, which directly worsens Blood stasis and pain. Gentle movement and warmth help move Qi and Blood, breaking up stagnation. Cold constricts and slows circulation, aggravating the condition.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold and raw foods that congeal Blood. Incorporate gentle daily movement like walking or yoga to keep Qi flowing. Manage stress with meditation or breathing exercises. Warm compresses on the lower abdomen can help during pain.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, fixed lower abdominal pain that worsens with pressure", "Fatigue and lack of strength even after rest", "Shortness of breath with minimal exertion", "Pale, greyish or dusky complexion", "Heavy, weak limbs", "Spontaneous sweating with mild activity"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and exhaustion, Prolonged standing, Cold, raw foods and drinks, Heavy lifting, Stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Gentle warmth on abdomen, Warm, cooked meals, Gentle exercise or movement
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's Qi is too weak to push blood through the pelvic vessels, the blood slows down and pools, forming the painful nodules and cysts of endometriosis. This pattern often develops after prolonged illness, multiple surgeries, or chronic overwork that drains your vital energy. The result is a dull, fixed ache that worsens with pressure, because the stagnant blood cannot move freely.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale with a purplish or dark tinge, stasis spots, teeth marks on the edges, thin white coat. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), fine (细 xì) and weak (弱 ruò), with a choppy (涩 sè) quality like a knife scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi deficiency means the body's engine is running on low fuel. Overwork, prolonged standing, and heavy lifting burn through that limited Qi, leaving even less energy to move blood, which worsens stasis pain. Rest, gentle warmth, and nourishing foods conserve and rebuild Qi, giving it the strength to push blood through the pelvis. Gentle movement like walking stimulates Qi circulation without draining reserves, while cold and raw foods further weaken the digestive Qi that is already struggling to produce energy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, and stews. Include Qi-building ingredients such as rice, oats, sweet potato, chicken, and dates. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax digestion and deplete Qi further. Gentle daily movement like walking, tai chi, or restorative yoga helps Qi flow without exhausting you. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, especially during menstruation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pelvic pain", "Pain worse with pressure", "Dark, clotted menstrual blood", "Irritability and restlessness", "Fever worse at night", "Dry mouth and throat"]

patterns.why_this_happens: When blood stasis lingers in the lower abdomen, it can generate heat, or latent heat from inflammation congeals the blood. This creates a painful cycle: the heat makes blood thicker and more stagnant, and the stagnant blood fuels more heat. The result is fixed, stabbing pelvic pain and dark, clotted menstrual flow.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, dry yellow coating. Pulse: deep (Chen), choppy (Se), and rapid (Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat and stagnation are the core of this pattern. Spicy and greasy foods add internal heat, making blood thicker and more stagnant. Stress and overwork stir up liver fire, which further heats the blood. Cooling foods and rest clear heat, while gentle movement helps unblock stasis without generating more heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling, anti-inflammatory foods like cucumber, celery, and mung beans; avoid spicy, greasy, and grilled foods that add heat. Gentle exercise like walking or yoga can help move Qi and blood without overheating the body.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pelvic pain", "Palpable mass or lump in the lower abdomen", "Copious thick or sticky vaginal discharge", "Sensation of heaviness or fullness in the lower abdomen", "Dark, clotted menstrual blood with heavy or prolonged flow", "Difficulty becoming pregnant"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw foods and drinks, Greasy, heavy meals, Sedentary lifestyle, Damp, cold environment, Stress and frustration
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Gentle exercise or movement, Ginger and turmeric, Stress management and emotional calm, Gentle warmth on abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it fails to transform fluids properly, leading to Dampness and a sticky, heavy substance called Phlegm. This Phlegm combines with Blood Stasis-often from long-standing Qi stagnation or cold-to form palpable masses and nodules in the uterus. The Phlegm obstructs the channels, while the congealed blood causes fixed, stabbing pain and dark, clotted bleeding. Together they produce the heavy, painful periods, thick vaginal discharge, and difficulty conceiving that are characteristic of this mixed pattern.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple body with stasis spots, swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating, distended sublingual veins. Pulse: choppy (Se) and slippery (Hua), often wiry at the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm and Blood Stasis are both stagnant accumulations. Cold and dampness congeal them further, while greasy foods generate more Phlegm. Movement, warmth, and drying foods help disperse the stagnation and restore flow. Stress tightens the Liver Qi, worsening blood stasis, so calming the mind is essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that create Dampness and Phlegm. Choose warm, cooked meals with ginger, cinnamon, and turmeric to move blood and dry dampness. Gentle, regular exercise like walking or yoga helps Qi and blood flow. Manage stress with meditation or deep breathing to prevent Qi stagnation.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure endometriosis?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to manage symptoms and correct the underlying imbalance, which can lead to long-term remission. Many women experience significant reduction in pain and lesion size, but it's a chronic condition that may require ongoing maintenance. With consistent treatment and lifestyle adjustments, some women remain symptom-free for years.

faqs.question: How long does it take for acupuncture to work for endometriosis pain?
faqs.answer: Many women feel some relief after the first few sessions, but significant improvement typically takes 2-3 menstrual cycles of weekly treatments. The goal is to reduce pain intensity and duration, and to restore a more normal cycle. Your practitioner will assess progress and adjust the treatment plan accordingly.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet for TCM treatment to work?
faqs.answer: While not mandatory, dietary adjustments can greatly enhance results. Avoiding cold, raw foods and inflammatory foods can help reduce Dampness and Heat, which often contribute to stasis. Your TCM practitioner will provide pattern-specific guidance, but even simple changes like eating warm, cooked meals can make a noticeable difference.

faqs.question: Can I take TCM herbs alongside my hormonal medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM herbs and acupuncture can generally be used alongside hormonal therapies and pain medications. However, it's important to inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you're taking. Some Blood-moving herbs may interact with anticoagulants or high-dose NSAIDs, so your formula may be adjusted. Never stop prescribed medication abruptly without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture painful? I'm worried about needles.
faqs.answer: Acupuncture needles are extremely thin - much finer than those used for injections - and most people feel only a slight pinch or a dull ache upon insertion. Many find the sessions deeply relaxing. The sensation is brief and far less intense than the chronic pain endometriosis itself causes.

faqs.question: Will endometriosis come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM treats the root imbalance, which can reduce the likelihood of recurrence. However, if the lifestyle factors or stressors that contributed to the imbalance return, symptoms may reappear. Periodic maintenance treatments and mindful self-care can help sustain the results long-term.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with endometriosis-related infertility?
faqs.answer: Yes, by improving blood flow to the pelvis, reducing inflammation, and regulating the menstrual cycle, TCM can create a more favorable environment for conception. Many women conceive after a few months of treatment, though results vary depending on the severity of the condition and other fertility factors. It's best to work with both a TCM practitioner and a reproductive specialist.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for endometriosis
research.description: Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials comparing Chinese herbal medicine to conventional therapies or placebo. Found that herbal medicine may be as effective as danazol or gestrinone in relieving dysmenorrhea and shrinking masses, with fewer side effects, but evidence quality was low.
research.periodical: Flower A, Liu JP, Lewith G, Little P, Li Q. Chinese herbal medicine for endometriosis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2012, Issue 5. Art. No.: CD006568.

research.title: Acupuncture for endometriosis-related pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: Meta-analysis of 10 RCTs involving 800 women, showing that acupuncture significantly reduced pain intensity on VAS compared to sham acupuncture or no treatment. Benefits were maintained at 3-month follow-up. No serious adverse events were reported.
research.periodical: Liu TT, et al. Acupuncture for endometriosis-related pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Pain Res. 2020;13:2489-2502.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for endometriosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: Updated meta-analysis of 18 trials evaluating various Chinese herbal formulas. Found significant improvement in dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and reduction of CA-125 levels compared to conventional treatment. Concluded that Chinese herbs are a safe and effective option but emphasized need for higher-quality studies.
research.periodical: Shan J, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for endometriosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol. 2021;258:123-132.
